title: The Ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
hookLine: he goes up and two men ask why they're staring at the sky
last: THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.

cards: You've dropped someone at the airport. You've hugged, they've gone through security, and you're at the big window watching planes take off, not even sure which one is theirs. You keep looking anyway.

Eventually somebody taps you on the shoulder: time to go. For forty days after Easter, Luke says, the risen Jesus kept appearing to his friends. Then, on a hill called Olivet, just outside Jerusalem, it ends.
He's lifted up, a cloud takes him out of their sight, and they stand there, eleven grown men, staring at the sky.

teach.b: Just before, they ask a question that shows they still don't quite get it: "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" Is it now? He doesn't answer the when.

teach.h: WITNESSES, TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: He gives them a job: they'll receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on them, and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, and Judea, and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he goes up.

While they're still looking, two men in white stand beside them and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" He'll come back, they say, the same way you saw him go.
Ascension comes from the Latin for going up, climbing. But Catholics don't hear it as Jesus leaving the building.

The Church teaches that he takes our human nature, wounds and all, into the life of God, and where he's gone, Catholics hope to follow. The angels' question isn't a scolding, it's a nudge: stop staring, you've got a job.
So they walk back to Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's walk, to an upstairs room, and pray together, with Mary his mother among them, for about nine days.
Catholic tradition calls this wait the first novena, from the Latin novem, nine: nine days of prayer.

teach.h: WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?
teach.b: Catholics keep the feast forty days after Easter, a Thursday, though in many places it's moved to the following Sunday.

how: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter (in many dioceses on the following Sunday), and many pray a novena, nine days of prayer, from the Ascension to Pentecost.

o: a monk's climb toward holiness, step by step
Jesus taken up into God's life after Easter
a raised step leading up to the altar

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus tells the disciples exactly when the kingdom will come
he doesn't answer the when. he gives them a job: be my witnesses.
the first novena was the wait between the Ascension and Pentecost
about nine days of prayer in an upstairs room, with Mary among them.
the angels scold them for looking up
it's a nudge: stop staring, he'll come back, and there's work to do.

games.q: you've just watched him taken up into a cloud. you're still staring at the sky. what happens next?
o: you wait on the hill for him to come back.
two men in white ask why you're staring, and you walk back to the city.
you all go home to Galilee.
games.why: "ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" they return to Jerusalem and pray together, waiting for the Spirit.

practice: If you can, look at the sky for a moment, or picture it, and let yourself hope, or wonder, or pray, whatever is honest.
Then bring your eyes back down to the room, think of one thing you've been putting off that would help someone, and picture yourself starting it. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Ascension. From the Latin for going up. Forty days after Easter, Jesus is taken up, and his friends are sent back down the hill to work. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a going up, a climbing. from ascendere, to climb.

carryVoice: Your line: why stand you looking up. There's work to do down here. That's day seventy-two.
